headline: Residents seek halt to Port St. Lucie assisted living project near petroleum cleanup site
teaser: Sandpiper Bay residents are asking city and fire officials to intervene in a proposed assisted-living development next to a known petroleum-contaminated property, citing engineering records that specifically reference the future senior facility during remediation planning.
body:
Residents of Sandpiper Bay are asking Port St. Lucie and St. Lucie County fire officials to intervene in a proposed assisted-living development next to a known petroleum-contaminated property, citing environmental records showing remediation planners specifically considered the future senior facility when discussing how petroleum vapors should be controlled.

The concerns involve PSL Westmoreland ALF, a proposed 150-unit assisted-living and memory-care development near SE Westmoreland and SW Morningside boulevards. City records describe the project as a two-phase development on 7.1 acres, with 124 assisted-living units planned in the first phase and another 26 memory-care units in the second.

The city's Site Plan Review Committee recommended approval Sept. 9, and city staff subsequently recommended that the City Council approve the major site plan. The proposal appeared on the council's Sept. 28 agenda. As of Tuesday afternoon, the city's online legislative record still listed the meeting minutes as draft and did not display the final action on the project.

The dispute centers on the neighboring Max Gas M LLC property at 2780 SW Morningside Boulevard.

In a 2024 response that later became part of Port St. Lucie's public records, environmental officials described Max Gas as a known petroleum-contaminated site and said soil and groundwater assessment activities were continuing through the Florida Department of Environmental Protection's Early Detection Incentive program.

More recent engineering records provided to Treasure Coast Today show remediation planners were already considering the planned assisted-living facility while designing cleanup measures for the gas station property.

A March 27, 2026 letter from BTEX Engineering documenting a pre-remedial-action-plan teleconference says officials discussed replacing biosparging with air sparging and soil-vapor extraction because of concerns involving surrounding properties where an assisted-living facility would be constructed.

The letter says that, for safety reasons, petroleum vapors would need to be captured during remediation.

Meeting notes included with the document similarly reference the surrounding assisted-living facility while discussing the proposed air-sparging and soil-vapor-extraction system.

Engineering diagrams accompanying the letter show proposed remediation infrastructure across the Max Gas property, including 21 shallow air-sparging wells, four deep air-sparging wells, 12 soil-vapor-extraction wells and underground remedial piping.

The documents establish that petroleum contamination exists at the Max Gas site and that engineers considered the neighboring assisted-living project when evaluating remediation methods. They do not, however, establish that hazardous vapors have migrated onto the assisted-living parcel or that future residents would necessarily be exposed.

In a letter sent Tuesday to St. Lucie County Fire Marshal Andres Elizondo, Mayor Shannon Martin and members of the City Council, a group identifying itself as the Concerned Residents of Sandpiper Bay asked officials to halt construction and conduct an independent life-safety review.

The residents allege that the assisted-living facility's proposed layout places vulnerable seniors too close to an active petroleum-remediation area and could create conditions that allow petroleum vapors or vehicle exhaust to accumulate near portions of the development.

They also contend that solid privacy fencing and the configuration of the proposed buildings could limit airflow around the neighboring remediation area. The residents characterized the situation as presenting a “High Risk for a Sentinel Event,” a term generally referring to an unexpected death or serious injury.

Those assertions are allegations made by the residents and have not been established by the environmental records reviewed by Treasure Coast Today.

The group also raised concerns about the location of proposed outdoor amenities and emergency access near the gas station property and asked the St. Lucie County Fire District to independently evaluate the project under the Florida Fire Prevention Code.

The residents asked the City Council to stop construction until the developer submits a revised layout providing what the group considers adequate separation from the cleanup area.

One part of the residents' letter appears broader than the available environmental record supports. The group said remediation personnel have no ability to address contamination once it crosses the Max Gas property line. An earlier environmental response in the city's public record says otherwise, stating that affected neighboring property owners would be notified if contamination were found beyond the boundary and that state-funded remediation could include contamination on a neighboring non-source property.

City staff's Sept. 28 project summary says the major site plan was reviewed for compliance with applicable city and planned-unit-development standards. Staff also said traffic and emergency-response analyses were complete and satisfactory after review by the city's third-party consultant.

Those reviews are separate from the petroleum-remediation concerns raised by residents.

Treasure Coast Today is seeking comment from the City of Port St. Lucie, St. Lucie County Fire District, the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and representatives associated with the development and neighboring remediation site regarding the residents' concerns.
